Journeys that changed history

Five travellers whose adventures changed the way we see the world.

A Ibn Battuta

In 1325, a young lawyer from Tangier set off on a pilgrimage to Mecca. He did not come home for twenty-four years. Ibn Battuta travelled about 120,000 kilometres, through North Africa, the Middle East, India and China, often working as a judge to pay for his journey. He was robbed, shipwrecked and nearly executed. When he finally returned, the sultan of Morocco ordered a writer to record his stories, and the book remains one of the most important sources on the medieval Islamic world.

B Jeanne Baret

In 1766, Jeanne Baret became the first woman known to have sailed around the world – disguised as a man. She joined a French scientific expedition as the assistant of the botanist Philibert Commerson, who was also her partner. Women were not allowed on navy ships, so she cut her hair and wore loose clothes. She collected thousands of plant specimens, including the bougainvillea, but her name did not appear in the official records. Her discovery was only recognised in 2012, when a plant was named after her.

C Matthew Henson

Matthew Henson was the son of farmers in Maryland and went to sea as a cabin boy at the age of twelve. In 1909, he was a member of the American expedition that claimed to be the first to reach the North Pole. Henson, who spoke the language of the local Inuit and was an expert at handling dog sleds, was probably the first to arrive. Because he was Black, however, he received little recognition for decades and spent most of his life working as a clerk in a customs office.

D Nellie Bly

In 1889, the American journalist Nellie Bly set out to beat the record of Phileas Fogg, the hero of Jules Verne's novel Around the World in Eighty Days. Travelling by ship and train with a single small bag, she completed the journey in seventy-two days. Her newspaper organised a competition in which readers guessed how long the trip would take, and nearly a million people took part. On the way, she visited Jules Verne himself in France, who wished her good luck.

E Tenzing Norgay

Before he became famous, Tenzing Norgay had already taken part in six attempts to climb Mount Everest. A Sherpa from Nepal who could not read or write, he had worked as a porter for foreign expeditions since he was a young man. In 1953, he and the New Zealander Edmund Hillary became the first people to stand on the summit. For years, both men refused to say who had reached the top first, insisting that they had done it as a team.

Which paragraph …

  1. 0.Who began their journey for religious reasons? (A)

Wolves are excellent travellers: a young wolf looking for (3) own territory can walk more than a thousand kilometres. In 2012, a wolf from Slovenia crossed the Alps and settled in northern Italy, where he found a female from the Italian population. Their pups were the first wolves (4) be born in that area in almost a century.

Today, wolves live in every country of mainland Europe, including Germany, France and even the Netherlands, one of the most densely populated countries in the world. (5) many people, their return is a sign that nature is recovering. Wolves keep the populations of deer and wild boar under control, and in doing (6), they help forests to grow.

In Slovenia and Italy, large white dogs live with the flocks day and night and chase (9) any wolf that comes too close. naloge.razlaga:
Kako rešiš to nalogo in zakaj so rešitve take
  • Kaj zahteva naloga: v vsako vrzel napisati eno besedo. Navadno manjkajo slovnične besede: členi (a, the), predlogi (in, on, at), vezniki (although, because), oziralni zaimki (who, which, that), pomožni glagoli (have, is, did), primerjave (as, than).
  • Postopek: preberi celo poved; ugotovi, katera besedna vrsta manjka. Nato preveri ustaljene zveze (depend on, used to, as … as).
  • Zakaj je odgovor pravilen: razlaga pove slovnično pravilo ali ustaljeno zvezo, ki zahteva prav to besedo. Kjer je več pravilnih rešitev, so navedene vse (ločene s poševnico).
  • Pasti: dve besedi v eni vrzeli; beseda, ki se pomensko ujema, a slovnično ne (who za stvari, that za vejico).

2. when

4. to

5. For
»For many people« = za mnoge ljudi.
6. so
Stalna zveza »in doing so« = s tem.
7. up
»make up for« = nadomestiti, odtehtati.
8. under
»under my pillow« = pod blazino.
9. away / off
Frazna glagola »chase away / off« = pregnati.
10. but / although / though
Nasprotje: učinkoviti so, a dragi.
11. freely / legally / again
Prislov ob »hunted«: freely (prosto) ali legally (zakonito).
12. because / as / since
Vzrok: mladi volkovi brez staršev težje lovijo divje živali.
13. in
»fairy tales in which …« = pravljice, v katerih …
14. whenever / when / if
Kadar le lahko: whenever they can.
15. rid
Stalna zveza »get rid of« = znebiti se.

Why food tastes different on a red plate

Most of us believe that we judge food by its taste. In fact, our (0) (EXPECT) of flavour are strongly influenced by what we see. Scientists who study the (1) (CONNECT) between colour and taste have produced some surprising results.

In one famous experiment, students of wine-tasting were given a white wine that had been coloured red with a (2) (TASTE) dye. They described it using words that are normally used for red wine, such as "berries" and "chocolate". Not one of the experts noticed that the wine was actually white. Their eyes had told their brains what to expect, and their brains had obeyed (3) (COMPLETE).

The colour of the plate can also make a difference. Researchers in Spain found that a strawberry dessert tasted ten per cent sweeter and more (4) (FLAVOUR) when it was served on a white plate than on a black one. In another study, people ate (5) (CONSIDER) less snack food from red plates, perhaps because we associate red with danger and (6) (WARN).

Food companies have long been aware of this. Orange juice is often coloured to look more orange, and many sweets would look grey without artificial colours. When one drinks company launched a (7) (COLOUR) version of a popular cola in the 1990s, sales were a (8) (DISAPPOINT). Customers said the drink tasted strange, even though the recipe was (9) (CHANGE) apart from the colour.

Restaurants use the same knowledge. Chefs pay careful attention to the (10) (PRESENT) of their dishes, because diners who are served attractive food are willing to pay more and rate the meal more (11) (FAVOUR). Some top restaurants even employ designers to choose the colour of plates, lights and walls.

The effect may also have (12) (MEDICINE) uses. Patients in hospitals often lose their appetite, and some studies suggest that serving food on brightly coloured plates helps them eat more. This is particularly important for older people with dementia, whose (13) (ABLE) to see contrast is often reduced. When their mashed potatoes were served on blue plates instead of white ones, they ate about a quarter more.

So the next time you sit down to a meal, remember that your eyes are tasting it before your mouth does. It is a (14) (REMIND) that our senses do not work separately but are (15) (CONSTANT) talking to each other.

You will listen to an interview with Grace Okoye, who runs a chain of bakeries that employ people who find it hard to get a job. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Interviewer: Grace, your bakeries are famous for their bread, but also for the people who work there. How did it start?

Grace: With a loaf of bread, really. Twelve years ago I was working in a bank in London and volunteering in the evenings at a shelter for homeless people. One night a young man there told me that he had trained as a baker but couldn't find work, because nobody would employ someone without an address. I thought, that's ridiculous – people need bread and he can make it.

Interviewer: So you opened a bakery?

Grace: Not immediately. First I borrowed a friend's kitchen on Sunday mornings, and he and I baked bread and sold it at a local market. We sold out in two hours. Within six months we had three more bakers, and I left my job at the bank. My parents thought I had gone mad.

Interviewer: How many people do you employ today?

Grace: About ninety, in five bakeries. Around two thirds of them have been homeless, have been in prison or have spent a long time out of work. We give them a full-time contract and training, and after a year, most of them move on to jobs in other bakeries or restaurants. That's our aim – we're a starting point, not a final destination.

Interviewer: Is it difficult to run a business like that?

Grace: Sometimes. People who have had a hard life don't always arrive on time at four in the morning. But I've learned that if you treat people with respect and give them responsibility, they usually rise to the challenge – just like the dough!

Interviewer: Do your customers know about your mission?

Grace: Many don't, and I like that. They come back because the bread is good, not because they feel sorry for anyone. We won a national award for the best sourdough last year, and that made the team prouder than any newspaper article about our social work.

Interviewer: What is your next plan?

Grace: We're opening a training school next spring, where people can get an official qualification as a baker. And I'd like to see big supermarkets buy from businesses like ours. If every supermarket bought just one product from a social enterprise, thousands of people would get a second chance.

A social entrepreneur

naloge.besedilo:
You will listen to an interview with Dr Tom Ashby, a scientist who designs sports equipment. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Interviewer: Tom, what does a sports engineer actually do?

Tom: We use science to make sport better, safer and fairer. That can mean designing a new tennis racket, testing football helmets or helping a cyclist find the best position on a bike. Last week, for example, I spent three days in a wind tunnel with a group of speed skaters, testing different suits.

Interviewer: How did you get into this field?

Tom: I was a keen runner at school, but I kept getting injured. My physiotherapist told me that my shoes were part of the problem. I was so annoyed that I started reading about how running shoes work, and I realised that I was more interested in the shoes than in the running. I studied mechanical engineering and then did a doctorate on the design of sports surfaces.

Interviewer: Has technology changed sport a lot?

Tom: Enormously. Think about the pole vault. A hundred years ago, the poles were made of wood, and athletes jumped about four metres. Today, with flexible fibreglass poles, the world record is over six metres. Or swimming: in 2008 and 2009, more than a hundred world records were broken by swimmers wearing new full-body suits. They were banned in 2010 because they gave an unfair advantage.

Interviewer: So where is the line between helping athletes and cheating?

Tom: That's the big question. Every sport has its own rules, and they are often decided by committees that include engineers like me. In general, we say that equipment should help athletes perform at their best, but it should not do the work for them. The skill must stay with the athlete.

Interviewer: Do you work only with top athletes?

Tom: No, and I think the most important work is for ordinary people. I'm currently working on playground surfaces that reduce injuries when children fall, and on cheaper running shoes for people in countries where most runners can't afford expensive brands.

Interviewer: What's the most unusual project you've worked on?

Tom: Probably designing a ball for blind footballers. It has small bells inside, so the players can hear where it is. The difficult part was making the bells loud enough without changing the way the ball bounces.

Interviewer: Finally, do you still run?

Tom: Every morning – in shoes I designed myself. And I haven't been injured for years.

A sports scientist

    A sports engineer.
  2. 1.What did Tom test in the wind tunnel?

  5. 4.What were pole vault poles made of a hundred years ago?
  6. 5.How many world records were broken in the new swimsuits?
  7. 6.Who decides the rules about equipment?
  8. 7.What must stay with the athlete?
  9. 8.Who are the cheaper running shoes for?
  10. 9.What is inside the ball for blind footballers?

2. His physiotherapist.
3. The design of sports surfaces.
4. Wood.
5. More than a hundred.
6. Committees (including engineers).
7. The skill.
8. People who can't afford expensive brands.
9. (Small) bells.

Kako rešiš to nalogo in zakaj so rešitve take

  • Postopek: pred poslušanjem podčrtaj vprašalnice; med poslušanjem zapiši samo bistvo. Vprašanja si sledijo v vrstnem redu posnetka.
  • Zakaj je odgovor pravilen: razlaga navede, kaj je govorec rekel. Sprejmejo se tudi drugačne besede z enakim pomenom.

Spodaj je pri vsaki postavki rešitev in razlaga, ki pokaže, kje v besedilu ali posnetku je odgovor in katero pravilo velja.

»testing different suits«.
2. His physiotherapist.
»My physiotherapist told me«.
3. The design of sports surfaces.
»a doctorate on the design of sports surfaces«.
4. Wood.
»the poles were made of wood«.
5. More than a hundred.
»more than a hundred world records were broken«.

»decided by committees that include engineers like me«.

naloge.besedilo:
E-mail

Your town's youth council organises an annual award, Young Volunteer of the Year, for a young person who has helped the local community. The awards committee is asking for nominations.

Write an email of 150–180 words to the awards committee in which you:

  • recommend and present the person you are nominating,
  • describe what he or she has done for the community,
  • explain why he or she deserves the award more than others.
naloge.rezultat: Formalno e-pismo s priporočilom: nagovor odbora, uvod z namenom, predstavitev kandidata, konkretni dosežki v skupnosti, utemeljitev, zakaj si nagrado zasluži bolj kot drugi, formalen konec; 150–180 besed.
naloge.razlaga:
Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. E-mail (150–180 words), formal style
  2. recommend and present the person you are nominating
  3. describe what he or she has done for the community
  4. explain why he or she deserves the award more than others
Kako napišeš formalno e-pismo
Formalno e-pismo: zgradba
  • Nagovor: »Dear Mr Smith,« / »Dear Ms Novak,« (če poznaš ime) ali »Dear Sir or Madam,« (če ga ne poznaš). Za nagovorom vejica, nato nov odstavek z veliko začetnico.
  • Uvodni odstavek: v eni ali dveh povedih povej, zakaj pišeš (I am writing to complain about … / I am writing to apply for …).
  • Jedro: vsaka iztočnica v svojem odstavku, s konkretnimi podatki (datumi, številke, primeri).
  • Sklepni odstavek: kaj pričakuješ (I look forward to hearing from you. / I would be grateful if you could …).
  • Pozdrav: »Yours sincerely,« (če si začel z imenom), »Yours faithfully,« (če si začel z Dear Sir or Madam) ali nevtralno »Kind regards,«. Nato ime in priimek.
E-pismo s pritožbo (complaint)
  • Povej, kaj si kupil ali obiskal in kdaj (I ordered a pair of headphones on 3 May, order number …).
  • Opiši težave stvarno, eno za drugo, s posledicami (As a result, I had to …).
  • Izrazi nezadovoljstvo vljudno, a odločno: I was extremely disappointed … / This is not what your advertisement promised.
  • Zahtevaj rešitev: I would like a full refund / a replacement. I expect … within … days.
E-pismo s prijavo (application)
  • Povej, kje si videl oglas in za kaj se prijavljaš (I am writing to apply for the position of … advertised on your website).
  • Predstavi se in navedi izkušnje in znanja, ki ustrezajo oglasu (I have been volunteering … / I speak English and German fluently).
  • Pojasni, zakaj te delo zanima in kaj lahko ponudiš (I believe I would be a valuable member of your team because …).
  • Postavi vprašanje, če ga navodilo zahteva (I would also like to know whether accommodation is provided).
Uporabne zveze
  • I would be grateful if you could … · Could you please let me know …? · I would appreciate it if …
  • Firstly, … Secondly, … In addition, … Furthermore, … However, … Therefore, …
  • Please find attached my CV. · I am available for an interview at any time.
Pogoste napake
  • Nagovor »Hello« ali »Hi« in pozdrav »Bye« v formalnem pismu.
  • Skrajšane oblike (I'm, don't, can't) in pogovorni izrazi (gonna, stuff, really cool).
  • Ena dolga poved brez odstavkov; ena iztočnica omenjena le v pol povedi.
  • »Yours sincerely« za »Dear Sir or Madam« (pravilno je Yours faithfully).
Ocenjevanje in postopek pisanja
Kako ocenjujejo pisni sestavek
  • Vsebina: ali si odgovoril na vse iztočnice (alineje) iz navodila in ali je vsaka dovolj razvita (ne le omenjena v pol povedi). Manjkajoča iztočnica je največja izguba točk.
  • Zgradba in oblika: odstavki, logično zaporedje, povezovalci (linking words), oblika, ki ustreza besedilni vrsti (nagovor in pozdrav pri e-pismu, glava in podnaslovi pri poročilu).
  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Zgradba e-pisma s priporočilom
Dear Members of the Awards Committee,
Formalni nagovor; konec »Yours faithfully« ali nevtralno »Kind regards«.
I am writing to nominate my classmate Luka Novak for the Young Volunteer of the Year award.
Uvod: namen in kandidat.
Odstavek 1: predstavitev
Luka is an eighteen-year-old student who has volunteered for three years.
Iztočnica 1: kdo je kandidat.
Odstavek 2: kaj je naredil
He set up free maths tutoring for younger pupils and organised a clean-up of the riverbank with over 100 volunteers.
Iztočnica 2: konkretni dosežki s številkami.
Odstavek 3: zakaj si zasluži nagrado
Unlike many, he does not volunteer for his CV; his projects continue without him and have inspired others.
Iztočnica 3: primerjava z drugimi in utemeljitev (What makes him exceptional is …).
I strongly believe he would be a worthy winner. / Yours faithfully, / Ana Kovač
Formalen konec.
Višja raven: 150–180 besed; ocenjevalci pričakujejo prepričljiv jezik (outstanding, tireless, a role model).
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
Dear Members of the Awards Committee,

I am writing to nominate my classmate Luka Novak for this year's Young Volunteer of the Year award.

Luka is an eighteen-year-old student at Gimnazija Celje who has devoted much of his free time to our community for the past three years.

Two years ago, he set up a free maths tutoring scheme for younger pupils who could not afford private lessons. Today, twelve students take part, and more than forty children receive help every week. Last spring, he also organised a clean-up of the riverbank, which attracted over a hundred volunteers and removed two tonnes of rubbish.

What makes Luka exceptional is not only what he has achieved, but how he has achieved it. Unlike many volunteers, he does not do it to improve his CV; he always gives credit to others. Most importantly, his projects will continue after he leaves school, because he has trained younger students to run them.

I strongly believe that Luka would be a worthy winner and a role model for young people.

Yours faithfully,
Ana Kovač

Število besed: 179 (zahtevanih 150–180). Zgled je eden od mogočih odgovorov; tvoje besedilo je lahko drugačno, a mora izpolniti vse zahteve iz navodila.

naloge.besedilo:
Discuss the importance of the island setting in William Golding's Lord of the Flies.

William Golding: Lord of the Flies

Write an essay of 250–300 words. Do not write about the text and/or the author in general.
naloge.rezultat: Esej s tezo o otoku kot preizkušnji, podprto s prizori (otok kot raj, brazgotina v džungli, ploščad in školjka nasproti Castle Rock, požara), in s sklepom, da zlo izhaja iz dečkov samih; brez obnove; 250–300 besed.
naloge.razlaga:
Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. Discuss the importance of the island setting in William Golding's Lord of the Flies.
  2. Do not write about the text and/or the author in general (no plot summary, no biography).
  3. Write 250–300 words.
Kako napišeš esej o književnem delu
Esej o književnem delu: zgradba
  • Uvod: avtor, naslov in teza, ki neposredno odgovori na navodilo (Will Freeman changes from a selfish man into …). Brez življenjepisa avtorja.
  • Jedro: dva do trije odstavki, vsak z eno trditvijo. Vsako trditev podpri s konkretnim prizorom ali kratkim navedkom in razloži, kaj pokaže (to je analiza).
  • Primerjava (če gre za dve deli): primerjaj neposredno z »Whereas …«, »Similarly, …«, »In contrast, …«, ne napiši dveh ločenih esejev.
  • Sklep: vrni se k tezi in pokaži, kaj pove o delu kot celoti.
Analiza namesto obnove
  • Navodilo pravi »Do not write about the text and/or the author in general«: ne obnavljaj zgodbe in ne piši splošno o avtorju.
  • Zgradba odstavka PEA: Point (trditev) → Evidence (prizor, navedek) → Analysis (kaj to pomeni za temo).
  • Uporabljaj sedanjik za dogajanje v delu (Will lies to the single mothers …).
  • Glagoli za analizo: shows, suggests, reveals, highlights, emphasises, symbolises.
Uporabne zveze
  • This is evident when … · A turning point comes when … · This scene suggests that …
  • At the beginning of the novel, … By the end, … · Gradually, …
  • Whereas X …, Y … · Both novels show … · Unlike …, …

  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.

Postopek v petih korakih

  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Načrt eseja
Uvod: teza – the island is not just a background; it is a test that removes adult rules and reveals the boys' true nature.
Teza v uvodu, brez obnove.
Jedro 1 – the island as paradise: fruit, the lagoon, Ralph's joy at the absence of grown-ups; the scar in the jungle left by the crash.
Prizori iz prvih poglavij; brazgotina napoveduje uničenje.
Jedro 2 – different places, different values: the platform and the conch (order) versus Castle Rock and the forest (savagery).
Prostor kot simbol: kraji ustrezajo skupinam.
Jedro 3 – destruction of the island: the first fire, then the final fire that burns the whole island during the hunt for Ralph.
Paradiž, ki ga uničijo sami.
Sklep: by isolating the boys, the island shows that evil comes from within, not from the outside world.
Sklep se vrne k tezi.
Merila: vsebina in interpretacija, zgradba, jezik. 250–300 besed.
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
The island in Lord of the Flies

William Golding's Lord of the Flies is set on a deserted tropical island where a group of British schoolboys are stranded after a plane crash. The island is far more than a background to the story. In my opinion, it is a kind of test: by removing all adult rules, it reveals what the boys are really like.

At first, the island seems like a paradise. There is fruit on the trees, a warm lagoon for swimming and no adults to give orders. Ralph is delighted when he realises that there are no grown-ups, and he stands on his head for joy. Yet there is already a warning sign: the "scar" that the crashed plane has torn through the jungle. From the very beginning, the boys' arrival damages the island.

As the story develops, different parts of the island come to represent different values. The platform by the beach, where the boys meet with the conch, stands for order and discussion. The dark forest, where Jack hunts, and Castle Rock, where his tribe finally lives, stand for violence and savagery. As more boys move to Castle Rock, the platform is gradually abandoned.

The boys also destroy the island itself. Their first signal fire gets out of control and burns part of the forest, and a small boy disappears. At the end, Jack's tribe sets the whole island on fire in order to hunt Ralph. Ironically, it is this fire that attracts the ship that rescues them.

In conclusion, the island isolates the boys from civilisation and shows that evil does not come from the outside world. The paradise is destroyed not by nature but by the boys themselves.
